items.title: I spent a month talking to Republicans and Democrats across America. They kept telling me the same thing
items.summary:
In the days after the midterms, we look at election maps for clues to why our neighbors voted the way they did. With Thanksgiving approaching, some of us will soon be sitting across from those same people, hoping politics does not come up. I have spent years asking a different question: What makes people sit down with someone they have every reason to avoid? 

I am guilty.

For years, I worked as an opinion editor at a national newspaper in the Netherlands. One day, I would work with a writer arguing one side; the next, with someone arguing the opposite. With every piece, the distance between them seemed to grow. On social media, their followers went after one another with growing fury.

At times, there was something almost bloodthirsty about it: the eagerness to mock, to scoff, to score the next point. And through my work, I was helping to feed that machinery of division. Eventually, I grew tired of it. So I went looking for an antidote to my own work. That search became The Divide , a book about friendships against all odds: people who grew closer despite everything that should have driven them apart.

For the past month, I have been traveling across the United States for the book, speaking with ardent MAGA Republicans and Democrats who called themselves socialists. What struck me was not how different they sounded. It was how often they said the same thing.

At the London Dragway in Kentucky, a group of Republicans pulled up an extra chair for me at lunch, let me climb into their race cars, bought me a T-shirt, and waved me off when I left. They told me Democrats were…
items.t: I spent a month talking to Republicans and Democrats across America. They kept telling me the same thing

items.title: Geoffrey Hinton said to stop training radiologists. A decade later, the Bay Area is 600 imaging techs short
items.summary:
In 2016, Geoffrey Hinton, one of the pioneers of artificial intelligence, said people should “stop training radiologists now” because algorithms would soon read medical images better than doctors. A decade later, radiologists are still in demand, and health systems struggle to staff the imaging teams around them. 

AI didn’t eliminate the occupation, but it may be eliminating the way in. If AI keeps absorbing the routine work beginners once learned on, preparation has to start well before the first job, and no single employer or school can build that path alone.

At the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), one of the Bay Area’s largest healthcare employers, we’re focused on developing more radiologic technologists, the professionals who perform X-rays, CT scans and other imaging exams. The regional numbers show why. The area has about 2,920 radiologic technologists, roughly 600 fewer than would be expected for a labor market its size, according to Lightcast labor market data. Lightcast estimates that over the past year, the region saw roughly one hire for every four job postings. The longer-term supply is thin, too: about 600 of the region’s rad techs are 55 or older. That pressure is unlikely to ease. The Bay Area is aging rapidly, raising demand for healthcare at the same time patients increasingly expect timely access to sophisticated diagnostic services.

The pipeline should start in high school, when most students pick a direction without knowing what the work involves. Ridgeline , the Bay Area nonprofit one of us leads, started a program called HealthX,…
items.t: Geoffrey Hinton said to stop training radiologists. A decade later, the Bay Area is 600 imaging techs short

items.title: Jensen’s back. What does that mean for Nvidia CFO Colette Kress?

Good morning. Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia’s CEO . But for Colette Kress, who briefly held the top job while continuing to serve as CFO, the leadership reset doesn’t necessarily mean a return to business as usual.

“We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s chief financial officer,” the company’s Monday announcement said.

But Kress was reportedly excluded from Nvidia’s board discussions on Sunday about reinstating Huang.

In my latest Fortune article , I examine what may come next for Kress, Nvidia’s CFO since 2013, who helped guide the company’s growth. A reported Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices adds another layer of uncertainty to an extraordinary stretch for the AI giant.

The precise focus of the investigation remains unclear, and an investigation does not necessarily mean wrongdoing occurred. Still, the reported probe raises questions about financial oversight.

One area drawing attention is Nvidia’s financial support for AI startups buying its chips, although it is unclear whether those arrangements are part of the SEC investigation. Kress reportedly raised concerns internally last spring about how borrowers were selected and how loan guarantees were valued.

Nvidia ( No. 16 on the Fortune 500), held its latest earnings call on Nov. 17. Kress said the company was “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” and would be “disciplined and selective in our support.”

Nvidia’s changes to how it…
items.t: Jensen’s back. What does that mean for Nvidia CFO Colette Kress?

items.title: Medicaid kids with autism are diagnosed at 5, then wait 201 more days for help
items.summary:
A mother leaves her pediatrician’s office with a referral and a warning that acting early matters. Now she has to find a specialist who accepts her insurance and is accepting patients. Make the calls. Complete the forms. Wait.

Months later, often years, her child receives an autism diagnosis. Then someone hands her another list of people to call.

We call parents who navigate this process tireless advocates. The compliment conceals an institutional failure. Autism care depends on families doing the unpaid work of making disconnected institutions function as a system. Parents pay with their time, income and exhaustion. Children pay in time without appropriate support.

Among children covered by Medicaid, the average age at autism diagnosis is five, and the average delay between diagnosis and treatment is 201 days.

When Dennis helped develop Diggy, which Esther supports as a founding advisor to its investor, Treehub, the goal was to address a persistent gap in autism care. Families often wait months for answers, while their children could benefit from support today. Diggy was designed to help parents take meaningful steps earlier, offering personalized guidance and activities that can begin before a formal diagnosis and support a family through a diagnosis.

Families can begin using Diggy the week they sign up, without having to wait for a formal diagnosis. Of the roughly 20,000 children who have used the platform, 60% started before age four and 75% before age six, with the average starting age just three. And in a four-week study of 91 children who used it, 72 showed…
items.t: Medicaid kids with autism are diagnosed at 5, then wait 201 more days for help

items.title: Current price of oil as of November 24, 2026
items.summary:
As of 7:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil is trading at $90.42 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s $1.63 below yesterday morning’s level and about $27 higher than where it stood a year ago.

Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $92.05 -1.77% Price of oil 1 month ago $117.47 -23.02% Price of oil 1 year ago $63.43 +42.55% 

Will oil prices go up? 

No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly.

How oil prices translate to gas pump prices 

When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds.

Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.”

The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve 

If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring.

items.title: Tech gets Jensen Huang back, but not with a clean slate
items.summary:
The tech bros are victorious. 

Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy led to his ouster from Nvidia . 11 days later, he’s back—the outcome Silicon Valley founders, watchers, and luminaries wanted all along. 

Within hours of Huang’s original (and ignominious) exit from Nvidia, a “Stand With Jensen” petition circulated online, demanding Huang’s return to the company he’d cofounded in 1993. Signatories included Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Atreides Management CIO Gavin Baker, and Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi, who wrote in the comments “Nvidia runs on Jensen! Bring him back!”

Travis Kalanick, Uber’s pugnacious cofounder and former CEO, was both a signatory and especially vocal in his support. 

“Jensen is one of the great builders of our time,” Kalanick—himself ousted in 2017 from Uber amid compounding scandals—wrote in a public post on the “Stand With Jensen” site. “Liberty and civilizational progress depend on Jensen,” Kalanick declared. “He has erred, yes—to err is to be human—but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company. Jensen deserves fairness in adjudication and we must presume innocence until that adjudication proves otherwise beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Huang’s return is a Rorschach test of sorts. Some critics see a corporate governance nightmare , while much of the wider public has memed or expressed horror at the circumstances of Huang’s initial resignation (widely described as borne of potential national security concerns). In Silicon Valley though, Huang’s ouster was…
items.t: Tech gets Jensen Huang back, but not with a clean slate

items.title: Stablecoins saved the day when Binance was exploited for $6.3B
items.summary:
The Binance hack was the largest exploit crypto has ever seen. Over $6.3 billion left Binance hot wallets on Oct. 29. However, this sophisticated and devastating attack was not an indictment of blockchain or the technology behind digital assets.

The underlying technology and blockchain rails performed exactly as they were expected. No chain was compromised, no protocol was hacked, and the vast majority of funds were stored in self-custody or cold wallets, all of which remained intact. A tokenization and wallet platform, Kresus’s self-custodial wallets were similarly not affected.

Much like FTX prior, this failure ultimately tied back to human fallibility. During the hack, roughly 17 hot wallets were drained in twenty minutes. This was achieved through an extremely sophisticated social engineering approach tied to malware deployments. So, this was less about the technology and more about a fault in operational security that the attackers were able to exploit. Fortunately, between $2.6 billion and $2.8 billion in funds were quickly frozen since these were stablecoins that issuers Tether and Circle were able to act on within hours to stop further damage.

New technology standards for tokenized real-world assets enable issuers and authorized parties to freeze necessary wallets and balances during the or compliance events. In other words, while the exploit exposed vulnerabilities in operational security and transaction authorization, it also revealed how the broader segregation of assets and role of stablecoin issuers helped limit the damage. The takeaway here is not the old…
items.t: Stablecoins saved the day when Binance was exploited for $6.3B

items.title: Women’s soccer has a $1 billion opportunity—and the CEO of England’s top two leagues wants a slice of the pie
items.summary:
The 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for women’s football, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers. More than 40 million people in North America tuned in to watch the U.S. beat China 5–4 on penalties in the final. Among them was ­ Canadian Nikki Doucet, then a student and college basketball player at St. Francis Xavier University. “That was the first time I’d seen women’s team sports on TV, and I remember feeling so excited,” she says.

Since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly. Its global fan base is projected to surpass 800 million by 2030, according to Nielsen Sports, while Fifpro expects the sport to be a $1 billion industry by 2027—a 72% increase from 2024.

Now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the company responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity. England has become a commercial force in women’s football: Eight of the world’s 15 highest-revenue clubs are in the WSL, according to Deloitte, and Doucet believes the league is well-positioned to capture a “significant portion” of the potential $1 billion the sport is predicted to generate.

American entrepreneurs and investment groups are taking note. The success of the Women’s National Basketball Association—now an $850 million franchise— underlines the potential, and many see an opportunity to buy in at an early stage in the commercial development of the sport.

U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL…
items.t: Women’s football has a $1 billion opportunity—and the WSL wants a slice of the pie

items.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
items.summary:
Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes?

In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north.

That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way.

items.t: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Incompetent or pragmatic? Nvidia board’s rehiring of Jensen Huang splits corporate governance experts
items.summary:
On Tuesday, Nvidia’s board chair said that Jensen Huang had violated the company’s code of conduct and that the former CEO had no future at the company . 

On Monday, the chair welcomed Huang back with open arms. 

The stunning flip-flop instantly made headlines and sparked a massive stock market rally, owing to Nvidia’s status as one of the world’s most valuable companies and the dominant maker of AI chips. It also brought immediate—and deserved—scrutiny to the corporate governance at the $4 trillion company.

Some governance experts slammed Nvidia’s board for its decision to rehire Huang as CEO, with one calling the board “incompetent” for its handling of his resignation and swift rehiring. But others said the board had little choice in the face of the plunge in Nvidia’s stock, widespread market turmoil, and pressure from shareholders and U.S. President Donald Trump.

“Morality and ethics just walked out of the back door for any large corporation,” Umesh Ramakrishnan, cofounder and chief strategy officer at executive search firm Kingsley Gate, told Fortune. “All the board had to do to advertise its incompetence was to reverse direction on the most monumental decision they’ve ever made together as a board within six days.”

The fact that several investigations have yet to be completed—including into Huang’s actions and reportedly into Nvidia’s accounting—added to the sense that the board acted rashly in reinstating Huang. But it also underscored the extent to which the leadership shakeup at Nvidia is light years away from being an ordinary situation.

That was made all…
items.t: Incompetent or pragmatic? Nvidia board’s rehiring of Jensen Huang splits corporate governance experts

items.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
items.summary:
On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels.

Continue reading...
items.t: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial

items.title: Cost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of properties
items.summary:
Rents to rise by 14% until at least 2029, Hamptons predicts, as high demand for properties and low supply push up costs for tenants

The cost of renting a home in Britain is expected to rise about twice as fast as that of buying one until at least 2029, according to research, with shrinking supply pushing up the prices paid by tenants.

Rents on newly agreed lets are forecast to grow by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared with house price growth of 7.2%, according to forecasts from estate agent Hamptons.

items.title: UK taxpayers held more than £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows
items.summary:
Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama, raising fears over cost to public purse

The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures.

items.title: Cloned number plate victims in England and Wales to get new reporting tool
items.summary:
Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties

Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned.

Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs.

items.title: The looming UK winter may spawn a double headache for Andy Burnham | Richard Partington
items.summary:
‘Raising growth in every postcode’ has been the PM’s rallying cry but deep regional disparities and rising energy bills pose problems this winter

Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year with rising inflation.

Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult.

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…

items.title: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout
items.summary:
New draft text released at Cop31 summit after countries fail to agree on electrification and finance for developing world

Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels.

The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress.

items.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
items.summary:
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
